content: Patients with mental health and/or substance use comorbidities can benefit significantly from interventions aimed at increasing hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment initiation, improving treatment completion, and achieving higher sustained virologic response (SVR) rates. Our review comprehensively examined all five major steps in the continuum of care for hepatitis B virus (HBV) and HCV. However, the studies included in this review did not focus on those with comparison groups. We employed the GRADE methodology to rigorously assess the quality of the evidence presented. Our findings extend the 2012 NICE guidelines on promoting and offering testing for HBV and HCV to individuals at increased risk of infection. The results demonstrate that culturally tailored educational programs delivered by lay health workers are effective in promoting HBV testing. All six studies reviewed showed consistently favorable outcomes, supported by relatively robust study designs, and were graded as moderate-quality evidence. Although these interventions were conducted among Asian immigrant populations in the United States, they may be applicable in other settings. The findings align with growing evidence that lay health workers can effectively perform a range of interventions traditionally carried out by trained medical personnel. The lay health workers in these studies received training to tailor educational interventions, and this training was both simple and low-cost. The cultural context and community-based delivery of healthcare interventions are critical for improving HBV screening in high-risk populations. Furthermore, the low-cost nature of these interventions makes them feasible for implementation in resource-limited settings. Our findings also highlight the effectiveness of clinician reminders during clinical visits in increasing HCV testing rates. These reminders align with broader efforts to standardize clinical practices, including provider-initiated screening and systems-based approaches to improving clinical outcomes. Coordinating care between mental health and treatment specialists, combined with psychological therapy and counseling for patients with mental health and/or substance use comorbidities, was shown to be effective in promoting HCV treatment initiation, completion, and achieving SVR. Hepatitis C disproportionately affects individuals with comorbid mental health or substance use issues. Historically, services for hepatitis, mental health, and addiction have been provided by separate clinicians or teams, often located in different facilities. While the interventions addressing multidisciplinary or integrated care in this review were diverse, a key contributor to improved outcomes was the co-location and coordination of services. Significant gaps remain in our understanding of progress along the chronic viral hepatitis care continuum. Implementation science in viral hepatitis will become increasingly important as access to effective HBV and HCV medicines expands globally. High-quality evidence is essential for forming guideline recommendations for program managers, clinicians, and other stakeholders. However, most of the included studies were graded as low or very low quality. The lack of robustly designed studies, particularly in HCV screening and HBV treatment, represents a critical gap. No studies were identified that investigated HBV treatment uptake, adherence, or viral suppression. Although we did not conduct an economic analysis of the value of incorporating operational interventions into the viral hepatitis care continuum, mathematical modeling in HCV suggests that imperfect follow-up during the care continuum significantly reduces the real-world effectiveness of HCV therapy. This underscores the importance of interventions that impact multiple steps along the care continuum, as they are likely to be more resource-efficient. Future research should focus on quantifying the costs and effectiveness of individual or combined interventions to optimize treatment outcomes. There are several limitations to our review. First, the outcomes studied were intermediate outcomes related to diagnosis and treatment, rather than disease endpoints such as morbidity and mortality associated with HBV and HCV. Second, nearly all studies addressing treatment uptake, adherence, and viral suppression in HCV were conducted with interferon-based therapies. Current direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens are simpler to administer, more effective, and better tolerated. In the DAA era, with nearly 100% efficacy, retention and progression along the care continuum are likely to become critical determinants of achieving SVR. Finally, all included studies were conducted in high-income settings, with the exception of one study from Turkey. More implementation science research is needed in lowand middle-income contexts, where the majority of people living with chronic viral hepatitis reside. Our systematic review demonstrates that a range of relatively simple, low-cost operational interventions can significantly improve engagement and retention along the chronic viral hepatitis care continuum. Additionally, we identified the importance of integrated approaches to hepatitis screening, care, and treatment for specific vulnerable populations. Further implementation science research, with robust designs and a focus on lowand middle-income settings, is needed to address current knowledge gaps and improve engagement and retention for people living with HBV and HCV.
